summary: Year 6 pupils learn to find a percentage of an amount (e.g. 15% of 360) by building from benchmark facts — 10% (÷10), 5% (half of 10%), 1% (÷100) — and combining them (15% = 10% + 5%), keeping the calculation grounded in 'parts per hundred'. The subtler skill is comparison: because a percentage is always relative to its base, comparing two percentages of DIFFERENT amounts requires computing the actual amounts, not just comparing the percentages. Anchoring to a 100-grid or bar, drilling the benchmark building blocks, and forcing explicit attention to 'percent of WHAT' when comparing are the core moves.
misconceptions: Compares two percentages while ignoring their different bases (assumes 30% off always saves more than 25% off, whatever the prices)
Misplaces the decimal when converting: treats 15% as 1.5 (or 6% as 0.6), giving a tenfold error
Cannot assemble a percentage from benchmarks, or takes 5% as 10% ÷ 5 instead of 10% ÷ 2
Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount rather than a proportion of the given whole

activities.title: Build a percentage from benchmark chunks
steps: Treat a bar as the whole amount (e.g. £360 = 100%) and partition it into ten equal 10% chunks.
Find 15% of £360 by taking one 10% chunk (£36) and half of another (5% = £18), then combining them to read £54.
Say aloud how each benchmark is found: 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 5% = half of 10%, 25% = ÷4, 50% = ÷2, and combine (e.g. 35% = 25% + 10%).
Record the matching equivalence each time: 15% = 15/100 = 0.15, and check the decimal point is in the right place (0.15, not 1.5).
Progress from friendly multiples of 5 to any percentage, and later to a single multiplier (×0.15) once the benchmark method is secure.
activities.insight: Finding a percentage of an amount is assembling friendly known pieces, not recalling an opaque rule; 'parts per hundred' stays visible on the bar.

activities.title: Compare mode: percent of WHICH base?
steps: Look at two bars of different totals side by side, e.g. an £80 coat at 25% off and a £60 jacket at 30% off.
First predict which deal saves more, then compute both actual savings: 25% of £80 = £20 and 30% of £60 = £18.
State the result: the COAT saves more (£20 > £18) even though its percentage is smaller, because the two percentages are taken of different prices.
Test the base explicitly: if the jacket had cost £100 instead of £60, recompute — 30% of £100 = £30 would now win — to show that the base matters.
Finish by writing a one-sentence explanation of why a smaller percentage can give a larger amount.
activities.insight: A percentage is relative to its own base; to compare two percentages of different amounts you must compute the actual amounts, not compare the percentages.

activities.title: Scored practice set with a base-ignoring distractor
steps: Complete fill-in build-ups: 10% of 360 = ☐, 5% of 360 = ☐, so 15% of 360 = ☐.
Answer a multiple-choice comparison of two discounts on differently-priced items, where one option is the 'bigger percentage must win' answer.
Use a slider to estimate a percentage on a 0-to-amount scale as a proportional sanity check before computing exactly.
Convert between forms in short items: write 15% as a fraction and a decimal and check decimal placement.
activities.insight: Fluency with benchmark build-up and correct decimal conversion, plus recognising when a percentage-only comparison is wrong.

activities.title: 100-grid reference and shop-context discussion
steps: On a 100-square where the whole grid is 360 and each cell = 1% (worth 3.6), reveal 10 cells (10% = 36), then a further 5 cells (5% = 18), then read 15 cells (15% = 54), as a benchmark reference.
Discuss a shopkeeper's competing deals on differently-priced items: 'which saves more?', and justify by computing actual amounts rather than comparing percentages.
Answer probing questions: 'How did you get 10% of 360 — and how do you know it isn't 3.6?'; 'Give me a quick way to find 5%, and 1%, of any amount.'
activities.insight: The 100-grid keeps 'parts per hundred' concrete, and talking through a real comparison forces 'percent of what?' into the reasoning.

checkQuestion: Two things, do them however you like and I'll watch. First, find 15% of 360. Second, two shops: a coat that normally costs £80 has 25% off, and a jacket that normally costs £60 has 30% off — work out which sale saves you more money.
checkAnswer: 15% of 360 = 54 (10% is 36, 5% is 18, total 54). Coat saving = 25% of £80 = £20; jacket saving = 30% of £60 = £18; so the COAT saves more (£20 > £18) even though its percentage is smaller, because the amounts are percentages of different prices.
